title: HIV and Hepatitis C Testing Algorithms: Acute HIV and Confirming HCV
summary: Apply the CDC HIV laboratory algorithm (Ag/Ab combination → differentiation → HIV-1 NAT), place RNA, p24 and antibody on the infection timeline, and confirm a reactive HCV antibody with HCV RNA.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 64 Hits 13 and 14 and Trap 3. Checked against CDC 2014 HIV laboratory testing recommendations (full PDF) and CDC 2013 HCV testing update (read via page fetch). Correction: HIV-1 RNA is detectable before p24 antigen (rv-hiv-earliest-marker). Hit 4 (HBV IgM anti-HBc, HCV SVR12) and Hit 6 (HIV viral-load monitoring; DHHS page not accessible) are not taught here.

objectives: Order the appearance of HIV RNA, p24 antigen and antibodies.
Apply and interpret the CDC HIV laboratory testing algorithm.
Interpret anti-HCV and HCV RNA results together.

scenes.title: Reactive screen, negative confirmation
scenes.altText: Two invented reports. HIV: a patient with a high-risk exposure 2 weeks ago — 4th-generation HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab combination immunoassay REACTIVE; HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay NONREACTIVE. HCV: a blood donor — anti-HCV REACTIVE. Question token: “False positive? Or infection the antibody test cannot see yet — and what about the HCV result?”

cues.text: Two weeks after a high-risk exposure, a patient’s fourth-generation HIV antigen-antibody screen is reactive, but the antibody differentiation test is nonreactive.
Separately, a blood donor has a reactive hepatitis C antibody test.
Is the HIV result a false positive, or an infection too early for antibodies? And does the donor have hepatitis C now?

props.label: False positive — or too early? Current HCV?

scenes.title: The order HIV markers appear
scenes.altText: A timeline (CDC 2014; schematic, not to scale): eclipse period — no marker consistently detectable; ~10 days after infection, HIV-1 RNA becomes detectable by NAT and rises to very high levels; p24 antigen becomes detectable by 4th-generation assays 4–10 days after RNA; antibodies follow. Definitions: seroconversion window = infection → first antibody detection; acute HIV infection = RNA detectable → antibodies detectable; established infection = fully developed IgG response.

cues.text: Right after infection comes the eclipse period, when no laboratory marker is consistently detectable.
About 10 days after infection, HIV-1 RNA becomes detectable by nucleic acid testing, and it climbs to very high levels.
Next, p24 antigen rises to levels that fourth-generation assays detect, 4 to 10 days after RNA first appears. Antibodies come after that.
Acute HIV infection is the interval from detectable RNA to detectable antibodies. During it, antibody-only tests are negative.

scenes.title: The CDC laboratory algorithm
scenes.altText: Algorithm card (CDC 2014): Step 1 — HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody combination immunoassay (detects HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and HIV-1 p24 antigen); nonreactive → no further testing. Step 2 — reactive → HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay; HIV-1 or HIV-2 antibody positive → infection confirmed. Step 3 — differentiation nonreactive or indeterminate → HIV-1 NAT. Interpretation: NAT reactive + differentiation nonreactive → acute HIV-1 infection; NAT reactive + indeterminate → HIV-1 infection confirmed by NAT; NAT negative + differentiation nonreactive/indeterminate → false-positive initial immunoassay. The HIV-1 Western blot is no longer part of the algorithm.

cues.text: Step one: an antigen-antibody combination immunoassay detects HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies plus HIV-1 p24 antigen. If it is nonreactive, testing stops.
Step two: a reactive screen goes to an antibody differentiation immunoassay, which separates HIV-1 from HIV-2 antibodies.
Step three: if differentiation is nonreactive or indeterminate, run an HIV-1 nucleic acid test.
A reactive NAT with nonreactive differentiation is acute HIV-1 infection. A reactive NAT with an indeterminate differentiation confirms HIV-1 infection.
Only a negative NAT with nonreactive or indeterminate differentiation means the screen was a false positive. The Western blot is no longer used in this algorithm.

props.title: Interpretation
lines: NAT − / diff − or ind. → false-positive screen

scenes.title: Hepatitis C: antibody, then RNA
scenes.altText: HCV card (CDC 2013): begin with an HCV antibody test; a reactive result must be followed by NAT for HCV RNA. A reactive antibody alone means current infection, past resolved infection, or a false positive. Anti-HCV reactive + RNA detected → current HCV infection. Anti-HCV reactive + RNA not detected → past resolved infection or false-positive antibody; usually no further action, but repeat RNA if exposure within the past 6 months is suspected, if there is clinical evidence of HCV disease, or concern about specimen handling; another antibody assay can be considered to separate resolved infection from biologic false positivity. Back to the hook: HIV → acute HIV-1 infection is possible; run HIV-1 NAT now (do not call it a false positive). Donor → order HCV RNA before saying “infected”.

cues.text: For hepatitis C, start with an antibody test. A reactive antibody must be followed by a test for HCV RNA.
A reactive antibody alone could mean current infection, past infection that has resolved, or a false positive. Only RNA tells you which.
Antibody reactive and RNA detected means current infection. Antibody reactive but RNA not detected means resolved infection or a false-positive antibody.
Repeat the RNA test if exposure in the last 6 months is suspected, or if there are signs of disease or doubts about specimen handling.
Back to the reports: the HIV pattern may be acute infection, so an HIV-1 NAT is needed now. The donor needs an HCV RNA test before anyone says infected.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Reactive combo + nonreactive differentiation = false positive” (✓ run HIV-1 NAT; NAT + = acute HIV-1); “p24 antigen is the earliest HIV marker” (✓ HIV-1 RNA is detectable first; p24 is earliest among antigen/antibody markers); “Reactive anti-HCV = active hepatitis C” (✓ confirm with HCV RNA).

cues.text: Trap one: a reactive screen with a nonreactive differentiation assay is a false positive. Not until an HIV-1 NAT is negative; a reactive NAT means acute HIV-1 infection.
Trap two: p24 antigen is the earliest HIV marker. HIV-1 RNA appears first, about 4 to 10 days before p24; p24 is the earliest of the antigen and antibody markers.
Trap three: a reactive hepatitis C antibody means active hepatitis C. It may be resolved infection or a false positive; only HCV RNA confirms current infection.

scenes.title: R-A-A: RNA, Antigen, Antibody
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “R-A-A — RNA, then Antigen, then Antibody: the alphabet of HIV infection.” And “Antibody says ever; RNA says now” for hepatitis C. Tokens: RNA ~day 10 · p24 +4–10 d · antibody last; HCV Ab = ever · RNA = now. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: R, A, A. RNA, then antigen, then antibody, the order HIV markers appear. And for hepatitis C: the antibody says ever infected, the RNA says infected now.
Where it breaks: timings vary by person and assay; HIV-2 is detected by the antibody steps, not the HIV-1 NAT; and a false-positive HCV antibody is never “ever infected”.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “HIV: combo Ag/Ab → differentiation → HIV-1 NAT if − or indeterminate · NAT + / diff − = acute HIV-1 · RNA first, p24 4–10 d later”, “HCV: antibody → RNA · Ab + / RNA − = resolved or false + · repeat RNA if exposure < 6 months”.

cues.text: A reactive HIV screen with a nonreactive differentiation assay needs an HIV-1 NAT because RNA appears before antibodies, and a reactive HCV antibody needs an HCV RNA test before calling infection current.

props.label: HIV: combo → differentiation → NAT · NAT + / diff − = acute · RNA before p24
HCV: antibody → RNA · Ab + / RNA − = resolved or false + · repeat if exposure < 6 mo

explanation.what: Plain language: early in HIV infection the virus itself is detectable before the body makes antibodies, so the lab uses a screen that sees both and then confirms in steps; for hepatitis C, the antibody shows exposure, and a viral RNA test shows whether infection is current. Scientific terms: eclipse period, seroconversion window, acute HIV infection, antigen/antibody combination (4th-generation) immunoassay, p24 antigen, HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay, nucleic acid test (NAT), anti-HCV, HCV RNA.
explanation.why: After infection, HIV-1 RNA rises first, p24 antigen follows, and antibodies appear last. An antibody-only confirmatory step therefore misses acute infection detected by the p24 component of a combination screen; NAT resolves it. HCV antibodies persist after resolved infection and can be falsely reactive, so current infection requires RNA.
explanation.measure: CDC 2014: RNA detectable ~10 days after infection; p24 detectable by 4th-generation assays 4–10 days after RNA; algorithm: Ag/Ab combo → HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation → HIV-1 NAT if nonreactive/indeterminate; NAT + / diff − = acute HIV-1; NAT − = false-positive screen. CDC 2013: anti-HCV → HCV RNA; Ab + / RNA − = resolved or false positive; repeat RNA if exposure within 6 months, clinical disease or handling concerns.
explanation.differs: Acute HIV (RNA/p24 +, antibody −) vs established HIV (antibody +) vs false-positive screen (NAT −); current HCV (RNA +) vs resolved/false-positive (RNA −).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: next step after reactive combo + nonreactive differentiation, order of HIV markers, and what a reactive anti-HCV alone means.

mnemonic.text: R-A-A: RNA, then Antigen, then Antibody. For HCV: antibody says ever, RNA says now.
mnemonic.explanation: HIV markers appear in the order RNA → p24 antigen → antibody; HCV antibody reflects exposure, RNA reflects current infection.
mnemonic.limitation: Timings vary by person and assay; HIV-2 is detected by the antibody steps; a false-positive HCV antibody does not mean past infection.

questions.stem: A 4th-generation HIV-1/2 Ag/Ab immunoassay is reactive and the HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation immunoassay is nonreactive. HIV-1 NAT is reactive. What is the interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. RNA (and p24) are present before antibodies develop.
Incorrect. A false positive requires a negative HIV-1 NAT.
Incorrect. HIV-2 would be identified by antibodies on the differentiation assay; the HIV-1 NAT is reactive.
Incorrect. The algorithm gives a definitive interpretation; delay risks missing acute infection.

questions.stem: Which marker is detectable earliest after HIV-1 infection?

options.text: HIV-1 RNA by nucleic acid test
options.rationale: Correct. RNA becomes detectable about 10 days after infection, 4–10 days before p24 antigen.
Incorrect. p24 follows RNA; it is the earliest of the antigen/antibody markers.
Incorrect. IgG appears late, marking established infection.
Incorrect. Antibodies appear after RNA and p24.

questions.stem: A patient has a reactive anti-HCV and HCV RNA not detected, with no recent exposure. What is the interpretation?

options.text: No current HCV infection: past resolved infection or false-positive antibody
options.rationale: Correct. Without detectable RNA, infection is not current; usually no further action.
Incorrect. Current infection requires detectable HCV RNA.

options.text: Acute hepatitis C in the window period
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeat RNA testing is reserved for suspected exposure within the past 6 months or clinical evidence of disease; neither is present.
Incorrect. Anti-HCV and HCV RNA test for hepatitis C only.
